section_title: How are worship and legal procedure used to destroy an innocent man?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Then Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab’s name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived with Naboth in his city. 9 In the letters she wrote: “Proclaim a fast and give Naboth a seat of honor among the people. 10 But seat two scoundrels opposite him and have them testify, ‘You have cursed both God and the king!’ Then take him out and stone him to death.”

11 So the elders and nobles who lived in Naboth’s city did as Jezebel had instructed in the letters she had written to them. 12 They proclaimed a fast and gave Naboth a seat of honor among the people. 13 And the two scoundrels came in and sat opposite Naboth, and these men testified against him before the people, saying, “Naboth has cursed both God and the king!” So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death. 14 Then they sent word to Jezebel: “Naboth has been stoned to death.” 15 When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned to death, she said to Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to give it to you for silver. For Naboth is no longer alive, but dead.” 16 And when Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he got up and went down to take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.

context_lines: Jezebel writes in Ahab’s name and seals the letters with his seal. She instructs Naboth’s local elders and nobles to proclaim a fast, give him a prominent seat and arrange for two men to accuse him of cursing God and the king.

The officials carry out the instructions. The false testimony is given, Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned, and his death is reported to Jezebel. She then tells Ahab to take the vineyard, and he goes to possess it.

The use of two witnesses imitates a safeguard in Israel’s law while defeating its purpose. [Deuteronomy 19:15–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/deuteronomy/19.htm) requires sufficient testimony and investigation of false accusations. Here the accusation and outcome have been arranged in advance.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/21.htm) emphasizes that the wrongdoing wears the appearance of both religion and justice. A fast and a formal accusation do not make the proceeding righteous.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/21.htm) likewise see the charges as a means to remove Naboth and obtain the property. The narrative exposes the cooperation of royal authority, local officials and false witnesses in carrying out the wrong.
god_plan_lines: The pattern of false testimony used to secure the death of an innocent person appears again in the proceedings against Jesus in [Mark 14:55–65](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/14.htm). Witnesses give false and inconsistent accounts, and the hearing ends with a condemnation for blasphemy.

This is a comparison of the injustice shown in the two accounts. Naboth’s story helps readers recognize how religious language and proceedings can be turned against the innocent. In the Gospel, that wrong is directed against Jesus Himself, bringing the need for truthful judgment into still sharper focus.
